items.item: A page has five parts (header, line-pointer array, free space, items, special space), and item identifiers grow from one end while item data grows from the other, meeting in the middle.

at.step: Reveal: a page's own five parts, read directly off a real table

items.item: A line pointer (ItemIdData) is an (offset, length) pair, 4 bytes, that never moves once allocated until freed, even when the item it points to is physically relocated to compact free space.

at.step: Reveal: a line pointer, decoded

items.item: A CTID (the row's visible identity) is a page number plus a line-pointer index, not a byte offset — this is exactly why a row's logical identity survives being moved within the page.

at.step: Predict: if VACUUM moves a surviving row to a new offset, does that row's own CTID change too?

items.item: The heap tuple header has a fixed size (23 bytes on most machines) followed by an optional null bitmap (one bit per column, present only if any column is null) before the real column data begins.

at.step: Reveal: the null bitmap, read off a real inserted row

items.item: A fixed page size (8 kB by default) is the direct cause of TOAST's existence: PostgreSQL tuples cannot span pages, so a value too large to fit is compressed and/or chunked into a separate TOAST table instead.

at.step: Reveal: a large value, moved out of line by a real TOAST

items.item: TOAST chunks a large value into roughly 2 kB pieces stored as separate rows in a side table (chunk_id, chunk_seq, chunk_data), triggered once a row crosses the 2 kB threshold.

at.step: Reveal: a large value, moved out of line by a real TOAST

items.item: InnoDB solves the identical fixed-page problem with its own overflow pages rather than a side table, and different row formats (COMPACT, DYNAMIC, COMPRESSED) store different amounts of data out of line.

at.step: Reveal: InnoDB's own overflow pages, the same problem solved differently

items.item: pageinspect's get_raw_page and heap_page_items are the real, direct way to read a live page's own bytes rather than trust a diagram — this topic should use them on a real page, not simulate one.

A page checksum and the pd_lsn field exist so a torn or stale page can be detected — named here, not taught in depth, since full treatment belongs to the next topic's own write-ahead-logging material.
This topic is the entry point to the whole chapter; every later topic (buffer pool, WAL, B-tree, MVCC, LSM) assumes the reader already has the page and slot vocabulary this topic introduces.
